Research record · 2019–2026

Machine learning for
strong gravitational lensing.

We develop models for lens simulation, detection, representation learning, image reconstruction, and physical inference.

Scientific problem

Using lensed images to study dark matter.

A foreground galaxy bends light from a more distant source into arcs and rings. Substructure in the foreground galaxy’s dark-matter halo can produce small changes in those images.

DeepLense develops methods to simulate these systems, find them in survey data, reconstruct image detail, and estimate physical properties. A central concern is how results obtained on simulations transfer to real observations.

01

Use known physics where it helps.

Lens equations, symmetries, and geometry can constrain a model without deciding the answer in advance.

02

Test transfer to observations.

Performance on synthetic images does not establish performance on survey data.

03

Evaluate reconstructions scientifically.

Image-quality metrics are not a substitute for downstream physical measurements.

04

Report efficiency and limits.

Model size, simulation cost, data requirements, and failure cases all affect scientific use.

Scope and limitations

How to interpret the reported results.

Most quantitative results in this collection use simulated or survey-like data. Performance on a controlled benchmark should not be read as an equivalent result on the sky.

  • “Euclid-like” and “HST-like” refer to simulation configurations.
  • Super-resolution may generate plausible detail that was not present in the observation.
  • Domain adaptation depends on a representative target set.
  • The hybrid quantum result does not claim quantum advantage.
